utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... We won't keep you long today. But I have to remind you that you are still under the oath. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let us resume our work. And my first question will be how many days did you hide in Mr. Milicevic's house, I mean following the 8th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hid there between three and five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I wanted to know, it was not more than five days, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never left the house, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can confirm that during those five days, your knowledge is based only on hearsay; you do not have any other kind of knowledge, do you from other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I wouldn't say that, other people. All the information that I had came from Mario Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, right. So it is other people. Whether it's Mario or Pero or somebody else, all the information that you had came from some other source. Tell me, after that, so it was the 8th May, five days is the 12th, and then you say that you joined the ATG, Benko Penavic. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But on the records, it's the 9th of May as the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in the house. How this came about, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Tell us, you said that you had green uniforms, that you were the only ones in the whole of the HVO. Is it true that you were the only ones with green uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they green uniforms which people usually called Israelian or Israelis because they had been imported from Israel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was green shirts and green trousers, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you invariably wore that uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not invariably. We had two different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you had two different uniforms. So which was the other uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camouflage one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And you are not aware that all of the HVO soldiers had a green working uniform and a camouflage uniform as a war uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please -- I will show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar, please, Exhibit 26.9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a pointer? Good. Will you please first circle the headquarters of the Convicts Battalion first. Wait, just a moment, until I switch on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, will you please do the same with the marker and put "KB" for the Convicts Battalion, Kaznjenicka Bojna.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is this big building, and I see you didn't circle the whole of it so --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it should be a big one, whether it's big or small, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean the building that you made a circle around.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, I promised that I would be very short, and I really won't have more than one or two questions for you still. But you can remove this. I've got the answer, and I won't be having any more questions about Siroki Brijeg. Tell me, did you ever see any paper on the basis of which you could get detainees, prisoners, from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did this paper look like, and what did it say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you still claim that it was Mario Milicevic's signature, rather than somebody else's -- no, let me first ask you this: Did you go to get the prisoners, you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used cars and trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the procedure? You'd go to the Heliodrom, and who do you report to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the person guarding the prisoners, and we take them over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Let's see like this. Was there a gate at the entrance, some guards there, or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who guarded that gate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guards, watchmen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, was it the HVO or the military police? Nobody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you -- you've gone to the gate and you get where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we get to the large buildings where the prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you went up in front of those buildings, and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we take those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Where do you enter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a man standing outside, and we say we need so many, say, for instance 30, and we take over 30 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who's that man standing outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the responsible person, the person in charge, or persons, I guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this man who stood outside, was he from the military police, HVO, or something else, and did he stand there and he said, "If somebody needs prisoners, let him contact me." How did you know who was the person responsible, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd really rather not go into all these details. I might make a mistake. And I don't really remember all these small details very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these are very important details, so I should really like you to recall them, because for the sake of the truth, you know. I'm asking you again, who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you say to these men standing in front of the building, "I need some men." And he says, "Fine with me. Take them." And you take them, and that's it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nobody made a list or anything, or did you make a list of those, or didn't you? Did you perhaps make a list, or did you just collect as many men as you needed and took them away simply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, now, who was the person responsible? If you went to get those prisoners, were you responsible for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- there were always two of us, more or less. I would always go there with another one. So we were -- we would both be persons responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the two of you should figure somewhere as the -- as persons responsible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the way from Heliodrom to the place of work and back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And can you remember the months when you went to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, was everybody like you, then go into the Heliodrom, find a man standing in front of the building, and you tell him, "Listen, I need so many. And he tells you, "Fine, get them. They're there." I mean did everybody did it that way like you, or was it only you who followed this particular procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'd rather not talk about other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now I will ask you to look at a photograph. It is Exhibit 20.9. Can you recognise any of these buildings as the one with prisoner -- housing prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll give you the Exhibit 20.4. And can you recognise any of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't really reproduce that image in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I -- Exhibit 20.9 [as interpreted], and can I... Do you have a clean Exhibit 20.8, please? Because mine is drawn all over, so I'd rather not use it. Thank you very much. [In English] 20.8. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here, can you recognise any of these buildings containing prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I simply cannot recall, and I'd rather not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, if I understood properly your testimony, in Mostar, you did not see any members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I? No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see them at the Heliodrom, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session, please, for one short question, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The defence of Vinko Martinovic has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But before this, I still would like to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Again, against this document. First of all, the quality of the document. We have the same quality of the document, so we are not to blame for a very bad copy. Re-examined by Mr. Poriouvaev:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And secondly: Witness, is it the second page of the same document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is exactly what I was trying to say. On the basis of this piece of paper, all you see is a police stamp at the border crossing - I think this is regulated by some international rules - and nothing else. So now we are getting some other suggestive questions. He's now saying, "Is this the second page of the same document or the back page of the same document?" So at least the Prosecutor should refrain from asking suggestive questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as we understand, that in all the passports or border pass, on any travel document, there are several pages. And when you pass a border control, somebody will stamp on that document. It's not necessarily on the same page. We believe the Prosecutor's question is totally [Realtime transcript read in error "irrelevant"] relevant. You may proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We have two different dates, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. There's a mistake in the transcript. I said it's totally relevant, rather than irrelevant. Relevant. Yes, please, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in addition to the suggestive character of the question, these are two separate -- different dates, and we don't know what this document is at all about this one. We only know it's a border pass which has to be attached to another -- or has to be a part of another document. And this is exactly why I cross-examined the witness on this point, to get this kind of a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you did not specifically bring up this point in your cross-examination, Mr. Krsnik. You missed that point. And the -- I believe that the Prosecutor during his re-examination will make it clear for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. If you take a look, there are annexes to the witness statement. Under number "6," you will see, permission for the trip Mostar/Zagreb, stating that it will have to go for medical control, two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I don't have this document. [Interpretation] I don't have that document. I have nothing marked with number "6."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It's has number ERN 02120136. And the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We have the document, but where do we find what you're reading out, that he was going for medical purposes? That's what I'm talking about. We have a series of documents which --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: ... controller.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course, I have to object, except in addition to my learned friend giving testimony himself, this is a permit of the military authorities for this person to be able to leave his unit. And these documents -- and we are still not clear what they are, even though I have asked more than 20 questions about it. This is a document with which one crosses a national border, so we should first clear this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear the answer from this witness. We believe that we have to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But I have not completed my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We have the document on two pages, in this way, this document was given to us by the witness. And as far as I see from this document, I think that we should give the -- a copy of this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, my question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: This document was on two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my question is whether you have that original document in your possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We don't have an original document. We also have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Where are those original documents? Yes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you ask the witness to furnish that document to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We will certify as to the copies made by the investigator who was interviewing the witness, and that's why we don't have the original documents, because the witness may still need them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have to ask this witness to furnish those original documents to your office so that we could know whether the second page is on the same document or not, because it seems to me there is some debate on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you furnish us with the original documents that is now at issue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would, however, like to request to have this document returned to me after it has been checked because I may still have a need for it. I think that I may have these documents in my hotel. And should you so decide, I can perhaps provide them later in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's a very good idea. And I can guarantee you that we will return that document to you after using it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I have got still two questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you return to page 12 of yesterday's transcript, lines 1, 2, the response to the Defence counsel question, the Witness said -- I am quoting. It dealt with the questions of logistic supplies and other issues concerning the command. "Whenever Baja left the town" - it was the witness response, according to the transcript - "he would tell us about what was his destination or, rather, why he was going there." Is it your response, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know to which places did your commander Mario Milicevic used to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several places. For instance, to Croatia, or perhaps to Siroki Brijeg to Tuta's, or it was to Ljubuski at Kravica, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And my next question will be about the solemn oath taken from you on the 8th of May, 1992, while you were joining the HVO unit for the first time. Were you present at this ceremony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who signed the document on behalf of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Yes, Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have a few questions, Witness AC, and they may not be in order. When you went to the Heliodrom to get prisoners - you said you did this a few times - did you pick the prisoners at random? Mr. Krsnik was asking you this, and I wanted to know, did you just pick the prisoners at random, go in and say, "We need 25, we need 30"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never at random.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So did you know when you went to the Heliodrom the particular tasks that were being carried out that day and the type of man that you needed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of specific tasks, but it wasn't really important what kind of man it was, whether it was older or younger, stronger or less strong. These people all had just one task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And that was filling sandbags and digging trenches and fortifications, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Making fortifications on the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, I know you were very young at the time, and it was a while ago. If you can remember, cast your mind back to when you went there, did the prisoners begin to associate you and your companion as people who had come to take them as prisoners to work for Benko Penavic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you perhaps give me a more specific question, because I don't think I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, we've heard from a number of witnesses that as prisoners of war, they knew and they had come to expect that they would be taken out to carry out tasks near the front line, and sometimes on the front line. Some of the prisoners have given evidence to this Court - now we obviously have to evaluate that - that there was a particular vehicle that came and a particular driver which made them very frightened, and they didn't like going with this particular driver. They associated him with something they didn't like. And that's why I'm asking you, did you ever get any impression that they associated you with Benko Penavic? Did anybody ever volunteer to go on your work force and avoid any others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer your question because I couldn't even look these men in the eyes, let alone try to understand their feelings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, again, I know that you were 16 or 17 during these events, but you were a local of the city of Mostar. You told us that you knew where Mr. Stela's headquarters were. Do you know what that building was before the war, before it became his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, you were asked yesterday about the destruction of mosques in the city of Mostar. In the period that you were with the military units and then the ATG, did you know of any reason that was offered, any discussion, about why the mosques were being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may not know the reason given, but I think that the goal of all this fighting and the war overall was to destroy the Muslims and anything that is associated with the Muslims in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to come to a subject that you're probably uncomfortable with, but I would like an answer. We know that you were injured I think in September 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is that -- or October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 15th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, we may have to go into private session for this, but I'll ask the question first. You described a conflict between your commander and Mr. Tuta, and you described how they had a meeting to resolve this conflict. Did that conflict have anything to do with the fact that there were Muslims on this particular ATG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you know what the conflict was? What the reason for the conflict was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. If you don't know the reason for the conflict, you obviously can't answer my questions. Did the conflict between these two men have anything to do with your leaving the country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Those are all the questions I had to ask you. And thank you for trying to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I have one question for you. After the 8th of May, 1992, you took part in a lot of activities of the HVO. What I was particularly interested in is the ethnic cleansing operations in which you took part. You described this operation in detail. You talked about violence and the theft that occurred after the expulsion, after the expelling of the Muslims. Could you tell me, remind me, who gave you these orders, and under whose orders did you operate when you carried out these operations? Who was your direct commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mario Milicevic, Baja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you please tell me, who -- Baja was under whose orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tuta's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. And I respect the fact that you chose to work for the HVO to save your own life and the life of the members of your family. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me Mr. Krsnik has a question. Further cross-examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first one question that relates to the questions asked by Her Honour Judge Clark. In -- when answering my questions and questions posed to you by the Prosecutor, did you ever talk about the conflicts between Tuta and Baja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give evidence in the last three days -- during that evidence, did you ever say anything about the conflict between Tuta and Baja Milicevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you're referring to. Is it between Mostar and Siroki Brijeg or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Judge Clark asked you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what Judge Clark asked me there. Can you please explain it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Clark asked you what kind of a conflict it was between Tuta and Baja and whether that was the reason why you left the country.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the country because I was not welcome, not even on the right bank where I took part in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were wounded, was that in combat or was it outside of the zone of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside of the zone of combat operations. I was -- I was wounded at a bend on the way from -- to Siroki Brijeg and Citluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So somebody shot at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shooting going on there the whole day. It was -- I was out in the open, and it was a very volatile situation there on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're trying to say that the bullet came from the east side? In other words, that the Muslims had hit you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make that assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is that from the -- how far was it from that intersection going to Citluk and -- than the first ABiH lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 300 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you were hit by a bullet fired from a machine-gun and that it came from a thousand metres, and that it was a fragmentation bullet that only was fragmented once it hit the target.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I was told. That is how things were explained to me. But the front line was -- the first positions were 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back. I find it difficult to communicate with you. Was it -- what did you testify about, a conflict between Baja and Tuta or Baja and Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was between Stela and Baja, but perhaps there was also conflict between Tuta and Baja due to the cleansing of Kozica, which from what I know, was something that Tuta did not allow -- had not allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is second-hand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are -- this is the information that I received from my then-commander Baja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, when Her Honour Judge Diarra asked you her question, you said that Tuta was Baja's superior. Yesterday you very properly said that you knew it and made that conclusion only on the basis of what Baja had told you, that you had no personal knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not go back to some --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. Sorry, excuse me, Witness, the question was: Who was Baja's superior? And you said Tuta. But yesterday, whenever I asked you, you said that you knew that because Baja had told you that. Is that true? That is what you told me yesterday all day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so. I answered very many questions yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes, but we talked about it yesterday. And several times when I asked you that, you said that you had no direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I worded it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. I do not have any further questions. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I just say something? You're absolutely right, Mr. Krsnik. I'm wrong. I'm reading my own notes here. And the conflict was between Baja and Stela, not -- but it was resolved by Mr. Tuta. I really am sorry. I'm sorry. Can I ask you again about that? The conflict between Baja and Stela is what you talked about yesterday. And did that -- did that contribute to your leaving? Was it about Muslims in the ATG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason -- I am not aware of the reason for that conflict, but that was not the reason why I left Mostar. I left Mostar for the reasons I have already stated. If you want me to, I can repeat them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: No, I don't. I just owed everybody an apology for the way I read my writing. And Mr. Krsnik was absolutely right. You did not describe such a conflict. And it's not surprising you did not know the answer. I'm sorry for causing that confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours. Just one more question, which now derives from Judge Clark's question, that there was -- that there was some friction and that Tuta resolved it. But we do not know whether it was Tuta indeed because this is the information that the witness gives us, and that is not direct knowledge. Further cross-examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the information I received from Baja -- I'm sorry that this man is not sitting here, but you'll have to ask about it elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'd like Baja Milicevic -- to see here in this Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'd like to does not really matter, does it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for coming here to help us by giving your evidence. We were sorry that we have kept you for so long. We wish you all good luck in your future. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the courtroom. And the last thing I have to tell you: That we request a representative from the Prosecutor with the presence of someone from the Registrar to go to your place to make a certified copy of that document to make sure whether the two pages are on the same document. We are expecting your cooperation in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you mean that someone from the Registry has to travel to where this witness lives to obtain that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the witness told us that he has this document in the hotel. He lived here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If that's correct -- it wasn't clear to me, Mr. President. But I certainly defer to your memory if that's what you think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may go now, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this moment, are there any documents to tender, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The documents are as follows: Exhibit P11.18/18 -- /11, sorry. /11. P14.5/12. P16.3/1. P14.3/7. P26.9/4. P15.2/2. The Documents P620.1, P621.1. As for the Documents P556, P588, P702, P774, they have been already tendered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual, Your Honours, we do not object to photographs. And for the others, again, as usual, I'd like to have three days -- or was it seven days? I don't really remember. Before we say whether we object to the rest of the documents whose admission is sought. But we shall do it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, now we are approaching the end of the Prosecution's case. And those documents have been extensively quoted, used, debated during the trial. We have kept this witness for three days already. We know your objections on those documents. We believe that we are ready to make decisions on those documents. They are not extensive ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honour. Some of the documents that were tendered, we already objected to those. I agree clearly. And the Defence should like to seek the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vinko Martinovic's Defence objects to 566, 588, 620.1. We object to orally. I do not know whether the Court would prefer us to object to them in writing or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par. I think I have stated our reason very clearly concerning of all those objections. Those documents are very simple ones. It is not so complicated, and we believe that we are in the position to make decisions on the admission of those documents. We rule that those documents are admitted into the evidence except that one we need some corroborations from the certified photocopies of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not tendered this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Are there any documents you are going to tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It is D1/40, which was PP14.5; D1/41, that is P590; D1/42, or P14.3; D1/43, or PP26.9. And now, one more document, which would be D1/44. That is all the documents that we were given as part and parcel of the statement, that is, attached to the statement that this witness gave to the OTP under a joint number D1/44, and... My apologies. Your Honours, Photographs 20.4, 20.9. And if our distinguished registrar could help me, the third photograph which has the number that Ms. Kimberly was kind to give up. I don't know which was the number of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those have been already admitted by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that. But what was its number, that photograph's number that Ms. Kimberly gave me that I showed to the witness? What was the number on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 20.8. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So I'd like to tender these three photographs showing us Heliodrom, and the witness was unable to identify any building, any of the buildings to which he went to collect his prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] I have another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And photograph Exhibit 26.9, that is the photograph of the tobacco station marked by the witness; that is, the witness marked out the headquarters of the Convicts Battalion on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is already D1/43.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Maybe it's not an objection, but I need some clarification. That's about the joint -- the document under the joint number. Mr. Krsnik means that it's all annexes to witness statements -- to the witness statement of this witness. But there are different kinds of documents in this -- within these annexes, including the document that already has its number and has been already tendered by the Prosecution. This is membership certificate. There may be some confusion then, because these documents has already its Prosecution number, 621.1, and it has been admitted by you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know. Perhaps we're talking at cross-purposes. I said all those which are attached and do not have their numbers. Of course, 621 has its number, so I don't mean this. I mean all the others which had -- do not have numbers and yet were attached. Do you want me to list all these documents? We were given the set. But I can follow the -- I can give you by quoting the Prosecutor's pages. I don't know. I'm in your hands. I don't know how to identify them otherwise. I noted down all the Prosecution's numbers on every page, or it might take too much time. Perhaps I should do it in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may submit those numbers to the registrar. Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I also would like to seek a clarification. When I objected to the Prosecutor's exhibit, I didn't mean those simple documents but three documents which are somewhat more complex in nature, and they are 566. That is the special report of the military police of the 3rd of August, 1993. I also had in mind P588, which is the report of the SIS of the 2nd of September. I also had in mind P620.1. That is Information A about the removal of persons of Muslim ethnicity from Centar II locality. And also I meant 702, which is, again, a report of the military police. Perhaps I misunderstood something. I do not know -- I'm not aware that these documents have been adopted. If not, then I'm objecting to them, and I can do it in writing as well. But perhaps I am wrong. So my question is, Have these documents been adopted, have they been admitted into evidence or not? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, the first document. What's the number of the first document? You told us that it's 566.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 556, P556.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I would like to inform you, by the decisions we rendered just now, those documents have been admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Then please receive my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since there is no objections to all those photos marked by the witness during these proceedings, we believe that all photos tendered by the Defence counsel are admitted into the evidence. And as for the statement of this witness - I mean the previous statement - Mr. Krsnik, you have to know that as usual practice, we do not admit the previous statement into the evidence, including its attachment. But we'll give it an ID number. And they're still alive in the document files. So when we evaluate those evidence, we will make reference to this document. It is so decided. Well, Mr. Prosecutor, how about your next witness? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be Major Rule. And there will be no protective measures. And I don't know what the Chamber -- we have ten minutes, but I'm happy to proceed either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll sit for another ten minutes. Then we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to make the best use of the time available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because we lost two hours for yesterday's sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's fine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Call in the witness, please. And are you going to brief us about relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President. And Mr. President, to answer the Chamber's question, this witness will give evidence relevant to the background portions of the amended indictment, paragraph 7 to 11; superior authority, paragraphs 14 to 17; and international armed conflict, paragraph 18. Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Major.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Rule, we've obviously already stated your rank. You are a major in the British army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've been in the British army for approximately 25 and one half years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, we've been both warned. Because we both speak English, we tend to question and answer in quick succession. So we'll try to both make a pause -- a bit more of a pause. Is it correct, sir, that your current assignment in the British army is you are the officer commanding urban operations wing?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to direct your attention, please, to approximately mid-October 1992. Were you a member or an officer of a reconnaissance party sent by the British army in connection with the peacekeeping mission in Bosnia in the area of Vitez and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just tell us briefly how you became involved in that and what you did in the month of October to carry out your mission.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I was part of the British Battalion which was formed to deploy on operations to Central Bosnia. That battalion sent a reconnaissance party in mid-October. And as I was a company commander in that battalion, I formed part of the reconnaissance party, and our job was to locate bases for operation once the main body of the British Battalion had arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if it please the Trial Chamber, this may be background, but I believe it goes beyond background. We object -- the Defence of Mr. Naletilic objects to this testimony based on the fact that it is well outside the scope and boundaries of this indictment and the geographic location of the counts of this indictment as pertains to Mr. Naletilic. We believe it's highly irrelevant. And we object on those grounds, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, I believe that the Prosecutor is asking some questions concerning with the background issues. When the witness first came here, I believe both the counsels have the right to prepare this witness into the situation. So we begin from October of 1992, and we'll see where the Prosecutor is leading us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, is it correct that the overall commanding officer of this British Battalion force was a British colonel named Robert, or more commonly known as, Bob Stewart?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there another senior officer involved in some role, during part of this time at least, known as Brigadier Cumming?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his role?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Brigadier Cumming was in command of the whole of the British detachment that was deploying to Bosnia, but Colonel Stewart was the commander of the British Battalion that was to operate in Central Bosnia; therefore, Colonel Stewart led the reconnaissance, although clearly Brigadier Cumming had an interest also in the reconnaissance as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you may have mentioned this a moment ago, but is it correct that as part of this initial reconnaissance effort, there came a time when the larger group left the Gornji Vakuf area and you stayed behind with a small group to essentially lay the foundation or do the groundwork for the later arrival of the main force?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That's correct. My own company, as part of the British Battalion, was assigned the area around Gornji Vakuf from which to operate, and that is why I remained behind there, to carry out further "reckies" for my company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that same regard, in fact, your company was known as the B - "B" as in boy - B Company of the British army unit known as the 1st Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you the officer commanding of Company B throughout your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I was officer commanding of the company until mid-January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you left sometime the second half of January approximately, is that correct, or perhaps mid-January?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Throughout that time that you were present, were you primarily involved in the areas around, as been mentioned, Gornji Vakuf and Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. And further -- further up the valley to Bugojno as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought it might assist the Chamber, but if the Court could look momentarily at Exhibit P3, which is the map of -- at least that portion, a large portion of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Mr. Usher, could you please assist me by providing the witness a copy of Exhibit P3. Should be a map, P3. If you can't find it, I'm certainly happy to let the usher use mine. There's a couple of marks on it, but I don't think it really matters. Usher, if you could assist me in such a way, if that could be placed on the ELMO, perhaps, is the easiest thing to do for everyone in the courtroom, and arrange it in such a way that Gornji Vakuf and Prozor area will be shown on the screen. I think with the assistance of the technical booth, we can probably zero in a bit more on the Gornji Vakuf/Prozor area. Very well. Very well. That's probably fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, those are -- those two municipalities and the surrounding region, that is the area that you were primarily involved in during your tour?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just point out - because this is not an area that the Chamber has heard so much about - within the municipalities, the approximate location of the town in Gornji Vakuf. There should be a pointer available, or if you can use whatever's handy to you.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the town of Gornji Vakuf. And could you likewise please show the Chamber where the town of Prozor is located.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Can you just, again by way of background, in connection with the case in general so the Chamber will understand this, was the Gornji Vakuf/Prozor area considered to be an important region because of transportation links?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. It was certainly an important area for the operation, for the UN operation. And it appeared to be a fairly key route further on into Central Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it considered either the principal or one of the principal routes from Croatia and Herzegovina into Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that is a leading and speculative -- that's a leading and suggestive question, and we're beyond background at this point in time. And I apologise to Judge Clark for having to make this objection, but I do believe it's a leading and suggestive question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, this question is not related to the indictment at all. We just want to know the situations there. Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us. Witness, you may answer this question.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It was certainly one of the major routes in, but it wasn't the only route in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally on this point, before moving forward in your testimony, if I can ask the booth's assistance please by zooming out so we can again see the larger area. All right. That's fine. Could you just, again, to orient the Chamber, can you point out in relation to where Gornji Vakuf and Prozor are located in approximately the centre of the screen now where such places -- can you point to the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you likewise then point to the -- sorry, my apology.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I wasn't pointing at. Yeah, there it is there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you likewise indicate to the Chamber the location of the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the main force of the British Battalion located in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, it's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness out of the room first. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, I was warned in no uncertain terms at the break that we are -- both of us are still moving too quickly in our questions and answers, so I'll ask you to assist in pausing a bit. If you can just think about -- maybe look at the transcript. When you see that my question has been transcribed on the screen in front of you, then perhaps that will be a cue to you that you can answer. And I'll do the same. It's my problem as well. Now, Major, will you tell us -- as you became involved in that region that you've discussed this morning, what were your principal activities during your tour there, your principal concerns?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Because I was operating from Gornji Vakuf, I had my own area of responsibility. And really our main effort was to try and create a climate within which we could allow the various humanitarian agencies to operate as freely as possible within that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it part of your standard duties to also liaise with, for instance, local HVO and local ABiH commanders and other local leaders?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Probably that was the most important aspect of the role which I believed we had. We had to try and create the atmosphere and the understanding in whatever way possible to allow relatively free movement of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to turn your testimony for the next few minutes to the topic -- to this topic. Can you describe to the Chamber, please, the role that information gathering played in the work of B Company of the 1st Cheshire Regiment during your tour.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Because of the -- the operational experience of the British army in a number of operations, we have found it -- and certainly my own battalion had found it important to gather information about what was happening in -- certainly within our own region but also broadly across the whole picture, because obviously everything impacted on what we were doing. So if there were local disagreements, then clearly that had an impact on how we could carry out our duties. And it was therefore important that we had as much information about what was happening, not only locally but -- but probably nationally as well. And we have a fairly tried and tested method by which we put in an infrastructure which allows us to gather information on what is happening. And the basis of that was that whenever we sent our patrols or whatever movement that our own soldiers took part in was always -- one of the main aims of it was to gather information on what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the term a moment ago "infrastructure." Was there a programme in place, if you will, or an infrastructure for the purpose of both collecting and recording -- and then I should add, reporting information?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Very much so. And again, our previous experience had shown how important this was. We therefore on earlier operations in other theatres put in place a system by which we could gather this information. The first thing we did and we recognised was important was to set up a small cell of individuals, NCOs, whose sole responsibility was to gather and collate this information for us. And the way that we would collate that information or gather that information was that any patrol or any person that was moving around the area would be briefed first by this small information section led by a colour sergeant, a senior non-commissioned officer, to obviously get them brief them up on what possibly they may be able to see and what may be happening around them as they went out on their various duties. Each soldier was given an aid memoir, a small booklet which had various different equipment types, had various badges, types of uniform which certain soldiers may be wearing. And certainly, as part of our training of our soldiers, we made sure that they were aware of what sort of equipment, what sort of soldiers they could expect to see. Once the patrol was at an end and the soldiers had returned to the base, they would be debriefed. The whole patrol would be brought into a small room, sat down. The patrol commander would have to produce a report, and the information cell would question the soldiers on the ground to find out whether or not they had seen anything of any interest. Often, what might not be interesting to a soldier or what he might not perceive to be interesting may have obviously other implications. So that is why each soldier was questioned, and all the information that was possible could be ascertained from that patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of this extensive process that you've just described, including the debriefing, would there be then a report prepared based on all of that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: At the end of each day, it was the responsibility of the colour sergeant in charge of the information cell to provide a written report to the battalion headquarters, which was based in Vitez. And it was then the job of the battalion information staff to correlate that information, obviously getting information from other areas as well, and send it as one principal information summary, which went to the headquarters of the British forces in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The particular report, the daily type of report that you've told us about, was that known as something called - and I'll spell this in a moment - a milinfosum, spelled milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a typically military abbreviated term for military information summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us in addition to those reports, the milinfosums, were there any other type of standard types of documents, reports, that were generated as part of the British Battalion's work?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: That would have been -- there would have been all sorts of different types of documents which we produced, but that was the principal vehicle in which we passed on military information. All the others really dealt with the day-to-day running of a military organisation. However, having said that, if a piece of information arose which was of particular interest, then this would be passed up immediately if it was considered important enough. And that would be in the form of what we call a sitrep, or situation report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, can you tell us, Major, the procedures that you've told us about just now for some minutes, was that unique to B Company of the 1st Cheshire, or was that standard -- if you know, was that standard practice with the British army units that were on peacekeeping mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: We were the first battalion that went there, so clearly there was no precedent in Bosnia. But I am convinced that that system would have been continued by the other British units which followed my own battalion through the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say, Major, that not perhaps in every detail that you've told us this morning but that type of information gathering and reporting would be standard British army practice anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. And more than that, each soldier, because of previous experience, would very much have that role inculcated within him. He would realise that every time he went out that an important part of his individual mission would be to gather and look for interesting information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, a couple of quick questions before turning to some of the documents themselves. As a professional military officer and as a person who was on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina in late 1992, early 1993, can you tell the Chamber, please, can you make any observations or give an assessment on whether the HVO, for instance, as you saw it, was an organised military force?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, it was an organised military force, and I was acquainted with the commander quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also give the Chamber any observation you can about, for instance, the quality or the effectiveness, for instance, of the HVO communication system?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it came as quite a surprise to me when I did see evidence of their communication capability. We, as an army, had particular problems with communications ourselves. And in fact, our only guaranteed communications out of Gornji Vakuf were through satellite telephone, Inmarsat. We attempted on numerous occasions to try and get a land line opened so that our soldiers could phone their families. And in fact, for the first several months of our tour, none of our soldiers were able to speak to their families other than through letter writing. I went to the HVO headquarters in Gornji Vakuf once to have a discussion with the commander, and we were talking and talking about families prior to our discussion. And I just happened to mention to him that I hadn't spoken to my wife for a couple of months, and to which he was surprised and showed me into a communications centre adjacent to the room that I was in and said if I wished to, I could phone my wife now. And I picked up the phone and phoned Germany, which is where my family were, and was immediately able to get through. In addition to that, I saw a number of different types of what looked to me to be quite sophisticated communications items of equipment within that communication centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment further, if you recall, on any other instance that you witnessed on the reach of the field communication?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And it remains very clear in my mind because we always had particular difficulty communicating ourselves. We used VHF radio, which meant that we really required line of sight to be able to communicate, which made it very difficult for us to communicate using VHF to Vitez, for example. Communications were always a problem for us. When the fighting first started in Gornji Vakuf at the beginning of January, there were a -- our first aim was to try and negotiate some sort of cease-fire, and I had all the commanders into my own base, and we negotiated a cease-fire. And I can remember clearly that a cease-fire of heavy weapons was due to come in to being at a given time. I don't recall the exact time now. As we were sitting in our conference room, this time passed, and heavy weapons continued to be fired. I then saw the commander of the HVO pick up a very small commercial-type radio and immediately send a message over this means. And I know that possibly eight, nine, even ten stations answered in very rapid succession, and this impressed me because our own communications were nowhere near as good as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the firing, in fact, cease after that time?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I think it was over the period that I was there during the fighting, there were various occasions where fighting died down but not necessarily completely ceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I didn't mean to suggest overall. But can you tell the Chamber whether as a result of that communication that you were telling us a moment ago, that there seemed to be a lessening of fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that question, the Defence submits, is purely asking for speculation in its answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, we don't believe that is speculation because this witness was there at that moment, but we believe that this question is a little bit irrelevant to the very issues. Mr. Scott, would you please lead us to the documents as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I didn't intend to stay on this issue long, but I did think it might assist the Chamber in assessing some of the HVO capabilities that have come up in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Major -- and I say this just because I think the Chamber should know this important fact of -- did you lose one -- a lance-corporal who was shot and killed while on a peacekeeping mission in Gornji Vakuf during your time?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, again before returning to the documents, during your tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it ever reported to you -- let me rephrase that. Was information ever reported to you about the sighting of members or components of the army of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. Certainly towards the latter part of December and -- and the early part of January, our information gathering was very much focussed on the perceived build-up of tension and pressure from the HVO. But also, I recall, my patrols spotting what they thought to be HV regular troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recall and assist the Chamber this morning with any particular details or any particular sightings of HV troops or components?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Clearly the detail of the military information sums is -- it is now ten years. But there are two occasions that I clearly remember. One was the sighting of well-equipped and well-dressed soldiers with a tiger patch on their arms, which a number of my patrols reported. We, using our own assessment, assessed this to be elements of the 1st Tiger Brigade of the HV. And also we spotted a number of command variant vehicles which would have had communications equipment which were required beyond the tactical level. They were higher than tactical level communications. And these were also reported to me through -- through the military information -- through my patrols, and which were passed on using the military information sums.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Chamber, did you ever have occasion yourself to meet with an officer who you assessed or concluded was an HV officer?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: After the fighting in Gornji Vakuf, initially our impression was that it may have been, you know, just a local instant. But clearly it gathered in scope and scale. And certainly on the second day of the fighting, we had representatives from both the BiH people in Zenica and also representatives from the HVO in Mostar. I remember one of the officers -- and I roughly remember his name. He was a very striking character. And we understood it that this chap was actually a regular HV soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll ask you why you thought that in a moment. But if you recall, can you give us this officer's name.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I remember it as something like Andric. But I have subsequently seen military information sums which say that that -- I didn't recall his name correctly. It was Andrejevic. But Andric, Andrejevic, was the name that I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I -- can you assist the Chamber a bit further that what was it that made you conclude that this was a HV officer.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Clearly military information works upwards and downwards. But it is our responsibility to brief what we saw, but it was also important for us to gain information downwards as well. And through those channels, I had it reported back to me that this particular officer was an HV regular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I should probably ask -- we talked several times this morning about the fighting in Gornji Vakuf. Can you tell the Chamber approximately the dates -- at least during that particular time period. I realise there may have been fighting more than once. But the time you referred to this morning, when was that fighting taking place?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The -- I mean, I was only witness to the first, initial, major breakout in fighting, because I subsequently moved on. But it would have been from -- from the beginning of January, perhaps 6th or 7th of January, where the real first incidence occurred, to when I actually left. The fighting was actually still going on as I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Because I was in the process of handing over my command to another officer, because I had been posted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is approximately the first half of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Major -- and if I could have the usher's assistance. If a blue binder of documents could be provided to the witness. The first exhibit, just by way of reference, will be P200.1. And I believe those have been distributed. For the most part, I think Defence counsel has those. I can see they're being provided to the Chamber now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can turn -- if you can find in the lower right corner, approximately, Major, the -- most of the exhibit numbers will appear about there. There may be some variation. But looking at P200.1, can you tell the Judges just in your own words briefly what that document is.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: This document is a milinfosum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm going to make this objection and ask the Trial Chamber in its discretion to allow a continuing objection if this is overruled. And the objection is this: This document, Exhibit P200.1, which I think has been given to Defence counsel and has been given to Your Honours also, is dated 16 December 1992. The witness has just testified before my objection that it was a milinfosum from that day, that is, prior to the term and scope of the indictment against Mr. Naletilic. And my objection will be it's outside the scope and therefore is not relevant in any of these other and further documents. Some may be in the time frame of the indictment that this Trial Chamber is concerned with. I believe there will be many outside the time frame. And that's my objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, those documents have been tendered already. Only because we cast some doubts about the origin, the form, of those documents, we did not admitted them into the evidence at that time. We also believe that those documents are dealing with the background matters, which is related to this very case. We'll hear what this witness is going to tell us at this moment. And at a later stage, we will evaluate all those documents. You can trust us. We can make the proper conclusions on those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I absolutely trust you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, if I can just add, so the record is clear, these documents all relate to, when they were originally tendered, two principal issues; that is, the existence of international armed conflict and the widespread and systematic nature of the HVO conduct and campaign which encompasses, in our view, and we submit and will submit, the conduct of these two accused. They are clearly relevant to this -- this time period is clearly relevant. The existence of an international armed conflict extends throughout this time period, as did the widespread and systematic nature of the conduct charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Major, I apologise for the interruption. But if you can look at P200.1, you were about to tell us -- I think I had asked you -- can you just tell us briefly what that document is.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: This is a milinfosum which would have been produced by the battalion headquarters that was based in Vitez. It would have -- it would have been put together as a result of lower-level milinfosums, which would have come from various sources, principally the three rifle companies that were operating in the BritBat area. And so if there was anything of any importance or notes of significance that had occurred in the Gornji Vakuf area, it would appear within this milinfosum, which would have been put together at the end of the day and forwarded to Com Brit For based in Split. It states clearly there that it's milinfosum number 45, clearly the 45th milinfosum which we produced. And the date which it refers to, 16th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you've anticipated some detailed questions I was going to ask you. Looking to the second page of that exhibit, is there a particular section -- for instance, because on the first page there's other areas, Travnik, Vitez. Looking at the second page, do you have a portion that includes the Prozor area?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: The paragraphs that refer to both Prozor and Bugojno would have originated from my company because we were responsible for operating in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
