utterances.text: Okay. Major, I'm going -- since you were on the ground for 91 days in Central Bosnia, I must ask you if you can describe to us, to me and for the Trial Chamber, the difference between an HVO soldier and a soldier from the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, the uniform that the HVO wore was generally the U.S. pattern DPM. It was similar to the U.S. pattern disruptive pattern material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that like camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, that's a generic term, camouflage. Disrupted pattern material is the term that you refer to on the combat uniform. This was markedly different. BiH soldiers wore a different style of DPM, disruptive pattern material. And you will see this in armies throughout NATO. There are a number of different types, colourings of DPM material. And broadly speaking. And again, there would have been a little bit of crossover. You know, sometimes somebody would have put another jacket on. But broadly speaking, the BiH wore a different pattern from the Croats, from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, as well as Mr. Witness, I have to remind you that you are giving a very difficult time to the interpreters. We all rely on the interpretations. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When I was a child, my mother told me to slow down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically, Major, both the soldiers with the HVO and the ABiH wore what you call generically camouflage uniforms. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: BiH, broadly speaking, yes. But these were irregular troops, and there was no sergeant major in the morning drilling them on parade and telling them off for having dirty boots or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've got to try to help the interpreters, and I'm about finished. The fabric was different, the colour was different, or the shading was different?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Both. I mean, all of those things. It's difficult -- and I'm sure it would be very simple to show the two styles of uniform. But the British DPM is different from the American DPM, which is different from the German DPM, in the same way the HVO DPM was different from the BiH DPM. The HVO DPM was broadly of the United States pattern. BiH DPM, disruptive pattern material, was broadly of an Eastern European style. It was slightly darker. And the pattern, the disruptive pattern, was different. And you could see at some distance the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major - and you have been in the army a long time - but when you got to Bosnia, did it take you a little while to tell the difference being a military man?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Well, when -- a little while, I mean a couple of days. The point was that clearly, at the very beginning, this was a new operation, and everybody was learning and learning very quickly. But it certainly wouldn't have taken us very long to be able to make the differentiation. And to underline that, I had been -- for example, I had been to Bugojno, which was in my area of responsibility, and they were fighting a particularly bitter struggle with the Serbs at the time in that area. And the two, at the time, the BiH and the Croat Brigades were fighting alongside each other. And certainly when we spoke to the two different types, that was where it very early on became clear that they wore two different styles of uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question, Major - thank you for your patience - during the combat in Bosnia, you were aware, were you not, that both the HVO and the ABiH army were able to buy on the open market the uniforms and that they could purchase uniforms from different countries and would do so?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Of course, and I think I already made the point that it wasn't a hundred percent uniform. But broadly speaking, there was a particular style of uniform that was worn. But clearly, as you say, uniforms were purchased from Germany, were purchased from surplus stores around Europe, and they were also worn as well. So it's not a hard and fast rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you still stand by your earlier testimony that it was difficult to tell apart the combatants at times because of the uniform situation?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. But, you know, it wasn't -- it wasn't in our -- for us, we were trying to make -- an accurate -- we were on nobody's side. We were just trying to get an accurate picture of what was happening. And so, you know, those deductions were - I would say, and still say - were fairly sound, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question, Major: The middle Bosnia area where you served your tour of duty, was it not surrounded by Serbs and Muslims? The Croats living in that area, was it surrounded by Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: There was -- I mean, we were aware of the broad breakdown of ethnic groupings in the Gornji Vakuf area. When you say -- you give a slightly wrong impression by your statement. And one of the great frustrations to me personally was the fact that when I first arrived, there was a lot of -- there was a very firm alliance between the people in that area against the common foe, and that was the Serb at the time, both in Bugojno and in Gornji Vakuf. Those forces were fighting side by side at that stage. And at the local level, the -- the coordination between the two sides was a very high level. So to say that the Croats were surrounded by Muslims and Serbs creates the wrong impression. They were -- both communities were under threat from the Serb at the time. So that was the impression that we got. And there was -- although the Croatian community in Gornji Vakuf was a minority, it wasn't an enormous minority. They were slightly smaller but not greatly so in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Major Rule, thank you very much. Have a safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just some clarification in regards of one document. Good afternoon, Major. My name is Mr. Zelimir Par, and I am one of the Defence attorneys for the accused Vinko Martinovic. I'm going to ask you some questions about a document that you had mentioned several times. I may not have fully understood everything, so please bear with me if I go and repeat certain things. This is P783. It is the last one in this clutch of documents. And my colleague has referred to it several times. And I'll tell you what I did not understand about this document. I did not understand what you authenticated in this document. Who is actually the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Again, because this is, you know, well after my experience, the organisation of our forces in Central Bosnia changed, and so I am unfamiliar with the originator of this particular document. What I can say is that it is a British headquarters which subsequently took command of that area. And I'm afraid that is all I can say. I can certainly see that it was initiated from a British headquarters because of the style and the layout of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, this entire document, which contains information received from these other battalions, was drafted or compiled by the British military authorities. Did I understand you correctly to have said that these other battalions were sending in reports to the headquarters; and on the basis of those reports, the headquarters, then, compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Having never seen this document before, and having looked through it now, I can see that there are replies from TurkBat, from CanBat. And if they are reporting back to those headquarters, those organisations would have been under command of that headquarters. Now, each information summary which would have come from those battalions would have been taken -- they would not have verbatim been taken into this document. The key elements as deduced by these headquarters would have been extrapolated and put into this document for onward transmission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this type of information which was coming from different battalions were verified in any way, or were they simply just straight forwardly put into the report, or was there any filter, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: There would have been a filter, in terms of verifying information. If it had been an information of particular importance, then I would -- I would think that there certainly would have been an attempt to verify it, if it was a key item of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at this specific document -- and you are here giving evidence as somebody who can authenticate this document. On the basis of everything that you have told me so far, this would be - how shall I put it? - an assumption or maybe an explanation of a regular pattern of drafting these reports. Now, do you have any specific knowledge about these specific documents, or does it simply follow the pattern that you're familiar with, of how these reports should have been done?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I have no specific -- I mean, I've never seen this document before, you know. I don't know it. As I say, it is -- it is familiar. Another thing I would say is that where somebody is commenting on something that they have seen, then it is clearly highlighted as a comment and not as a specific fact which had been witnessed on the ground by -- by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me try to be as direct as I can. Are you in a position or are you the right person who could authenticate this document to us, or is this document slightly different from the other documents that you discussed here today?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: It is different, because it's initiated at a higher level. I was only involved in documents that were produced at unit level, at our battalion level. I never worked at a brigade level, which is probably what this roughly equates to, in Gornji Vakuf or during my tour of duty there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major. I have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just thought, Major, that we owed it to you to explain why it was necessary for you to come in relation to these documents. We were concerned that they had no apparent visible provenance on them, they had no signature, and they had no stamp from an army base. I think I see your explanations, communications were difficult. And the documents probably went by telex, did they?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: Absolutely. It would have been impractical to have them personally signed and sent. These would have initially used fax in the early days and then telex and, you know, other electronic media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. You see the documents that we had seen from the other battalions were faxed and obviously were on official paper. And that's why we were concerned. But you've resolved our concerns. Major, there was just one very, very short question. You may not be able to answer this. You may not be able to assist. But perhaps you can. At least one witness, possibly two witnesses, have given evidence in the past of being asked to bury bodies. And these witnesses were prisoners, and therefore communications with the people giving orders would have been, to say the least, limited. And they noticed that sometimes when they were burying bodies, that the bodies wore boots of an exceptionally high quality, totally different, they said, from the boots they were used to. And they identified those boots as being on the bodies of Croatian army soldiers, in other words, HV soldiers. Do you have any comment at all about the footwear between HV soldiers and HVO and, of course, Armija?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR RULE
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't recall anything. Anything I say would just -- be just conjecture, other than many of these people had access to Germany and clearly would have been able to get hold of items or equipment that might make -- might have made their life a bit more comfortable, i.e., they were warmer and -- but specifically, I can't recall anything specifically about boots in my time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's question? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to help us. We all wish you a pleasant trip back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, are there any documents you are going to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, we would tender -- and I'm going to because of the Court's prior questions, which I appreciate -- I'm going to tender the -- some of the documents again, just to make sure that on the basis of this additional evidence, the record will be clear that they've been tendered. We tender P200.1, P208.1, IAC-26, P216.1, IAC-63, IAC-66, IAC-75, P364, and P783.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe all those documents have been tendered before but pending a decision from this Trial Chamber. Are there any objections? Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Vinko Martinovic opposes the P783 being entered in evidence because we believe that this witness is not the right kind of witness to authorise -- to authenticate this type of document. We cannot see how -- who actually authored this document, how it was compiled. All he was able to say about this document were conjectures, assumptions. And also it was an extemporaneous document. In other words, it was not compiled at the time when he was there on duty. And since the -- and this will be our objection. In case that the Defence of the first accused has objections to other document, we would second their objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe that the Defence for Mladen Naletilic has previously filed objections to these documents, which we would reiterate. We believe they're outside the scope of the indictment. And specifically on Exhibit P783, this was a document generated in August of 1994, seven months or more after the time of this indictment. I want to point that specifically out to the Court. But I believe that we have heretofore entered written objections to those documents. We would reiterate those same objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultations among the Judges, we have made a decision on the admission of those evidence. Since all those documents have been tendered before, and since we have been seized by the motion filed by the Defence counsel objecting the admission of these documents, we would like to say that all these documents have been admitted into the evidence except that document P783. We believe that this document is not in the same category with the other documents. It is so decided. Yes, Mr. Scott. Do you have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'd like to call the next witness. And it will be protected -- it will be a protected witness, so I won't be in a position -- perhaps we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please bring in the Witness, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is a test. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Witness, I'm not using your name because the protective measures that you have requested have been granted, and that is you are testifying using a pseudonym instead of your true name, and your facial image is being protected. Therefore, we need to make a record of the person that, in fact, you are. And in order to do that, a name has been put on a paper that the usher is showing you now. And I want to start by asking you -- don't say your name. But if you look at the paper, you can just say "yes" or "no", is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In connection with your protective measures, Witness AD, let me just say again -- and let me indicate, when I say "Witness AD", that is the pseudonym that has been assigned to you. It will be important in the course of your testimony if you can try to remember not to mention family names or information which might tend to identify you. If there's a need for that, or a name or some other detail, we will try to go into private session so that you can say -- give answers to those questions in a way that no one outside the courtroom will be able to hear that information. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Witness AD, I want to say personally before we start, I apologise for the long delay in having you come into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to start, please, with some background identification, if we could go into private session for the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AD, can you tell the Chamber, please, on the 9th of May, 1993, at about 5.00 in the morning, were you in your flat with your family when the HVO attacked Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber whether you were surprised at this attack, or did you have any sort of information or impression that this attack was coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Oh, I was quite taken by surprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see or what did you hear or see happening, very briefly? Because I will tell you that the Chamber has heard a fair amount of evidence on this point. But from your personal perspective, what could you see and hear going on around you on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: It was in the morning at 20 to 5.00, from the hill of Hum above Mostar, they opened fire. I looked through the window, and I could see that the streets were awash with people, Muslims were en masse expelled from their flats, and they took them to the Velez stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any HVO soldiers come to your flat on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes. At 7.00, he came and took my husband and my two sons away. But then he recognised him and brought him back again so that they stayed in the flat until 12.00 on the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So just so your evidence is clear, because it seemed to indicate initially your husband and sons were taken away but then they were brought back. Can you just perhaps be a bit clearer on what happened in that regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: I suppose somebody recognised my husband. I mean one of those soldiers must have recognised my husband, because my sons had already come down the stairs. And they asked my husband, "Who is this"? And he said, "These are my two sons". And they came back then, and nobody came to our apartment again until 12.00 the next day, the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, and that's what I wanted to go to next, please. At approximately 12.00 the next day, on the 10th of May, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Like this: At 12.00 on the 10th of May, Danko Carapina in a black uniform came to the door. He said to my husband to follow him. I was in the doorway of our living room, and he ordered me to get back into the living room and told me that if I looked to see where they were taking him, that they would open fire on the flat or throw zolja at it. My husband wanted to take a cardigan with him, and this man told him that he would not need it and fired between the two of us in the anteroom, and this bullet went through our freezer and hit a cupboard in the passageway. But we saw that only later on. And he took my husband away. Then came back 15 minutes later to get my son. He ordered him to turn face to the wall, told him to put his hands up, and asked me "Where's that fair-haired woman"? And I said, "I guess you mean me. I'm his mother." He had two more soldiers with him. They took my son away. And I did not know anything else about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions about your answer just now. The HVO soldier who came to your house at approximately noon on the 10th of May, I'm just looking at the transcript, just so we're clear, and if you can, can you spell his first name and his last name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: To spell it, C-a-r-a-p-i-n-a. First name, D-a-n-k-o.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First name Danko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that same soldier came back after first taking your husband away and took one of your sons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the older son that was taken away at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the older one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, just so the record is complete, where was your younger son at that time, in general terms? And again, don't name names. But where was your younger son?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: My younger son was in the flat of one of his friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn at that time or come to know later where both your husband and your older son were taken after they were taken from your flat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: I found that out the next day. I learned that they were at the Heliodrom, or rather -- sorry, first, they took them to the mechanical engineering faculty, and they were kept there until midnight or 1.00 in the morning. And the next morning, they were taken to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, staying, again, on the 10th of May, can you tell us whether this same HVO soldier came back to your flat still again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: He did, yes. He came back to my flat half an hour later and requested the keys to the flat and to the garage. He went back to the garage and drove away the car and seized all the keys I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive your car back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 9th and 10th of May, and again without naming any names, the area where you lived, were you surrounded by a number of Croat families or Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while your husband and older son and others were being taken away, did you see any of the Croat families being taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AD, I want to direct your attention to the following day, the 11th of May. Does someone come to your house with some information for you on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes. At 6.00 in the afternoon, three soldiers came. I did not know them. And they did not tell me their names, but one of them said that my husband had sent for the motorbike, so I went downstairs and took out the motorbike. And they drove it away. I just asked one of them "What has happened to my husband"? And he said, "You'll find that out in ten days." And I'm sorry, but I have to add this, too: He also said, "Your husband did not fair well [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did anyone else come to your apartment on the 11th of May around that time, besides these three men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct, Witness AD, that your husband and your older son were then held at the Heliodrom for approximately the next ten days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that time, did your husband and your older son return to your flat -- return to you in your flat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AD, I only want to touch on this briefly, but did either your husband or your older son give you any information about what had happened to them, what they had seen or heard when they were being held at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes. Both my husband and my son told me that there were about three or four hundred people in the large hall. They were all put up there. My husband was beaten up then. His ribs were broken. He had big wounds on his knees. His trousers were torn. He was black and blue Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 8180 to 8184. around his eyes. And their nerves were in very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband and your older son then continue to live, the three of you - and your younger son - continue to live in your flat, then, together until approximately the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber on the 30th of June, 1993 what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, 1993, at 8.00 in the evening, they took away all the Muslim men from their flats. They went to all the state cases [as interpreted], to all the houses, and rounded them up and took them all to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- before that -- let me go back for a moment. Between the time that your husband was released from the Heliodrom and the time when he was arrested again, on the 30th of June, did he say anything to you about any fears that he had or any encounters or meetings that he had had with any persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Like this: Between the 9th of May, until the 30th of June, they dared not go out into the street. And most of us stayed in our houses, in our flats, because Croat troops were around our buildings all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. During that time, Witness AD, did your husband say anything to you that he was afraid of any particular person and he feared that something would happen to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll have to -- I see your head nodding in the affirmative, but you'll have to give a verbal response.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My husband had been to see my aunt who lived across the street from Stela's space. And on his way back, on the bicycle, he came back, he was very pale, and started smoking one cigarette after the other, walking up and down the house, and saying, "I've just seen Stela. He'll kill me." He was very upset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband explain to you at that time what the basis for him saying that was, what had happened, or what the circumstances were, that caused him to say that "he'll" -- meaning -- referring to Stela, "He'll kill me"? Do you know why he said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: He was riding a bicycle, and Stela said -- that is, he addressed him by his name and said, "Where are you, thief?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to after, then, your husband was arrested on the 30th of June. Again, did you know or come to know where he was taken at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: I found it out on the 30th of June in the morning that they had taken him to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of your two sons, which again we won't use their names, did your old -- your older son avoided being arrested on the 30th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, without using any names, where was he on the 30th of June which prevented him from -- or at least, he was not arrested that day? Where was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AD
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, immediately after my husband's arrest, we took him to a locality across the street from Stela's building to his girlfriend's, and he hid there in the loft for ten days. And my younger son was on Husinska Buna Street at his friend's, whose mother was a Croat and father a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to start on a different series of questions, and I would suggest that that might be a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness out of the room first, after pulling down the blinds. Witness, I'm afraid we have to keep you here for another day. As I did with other witnesses, during your stay here, do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may go now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the Chamber arrives --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. Before the Chamber rises, could I have one moment of your time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will not be very popular for raising this subject, but I feel that I've been required to. I don't know if the Chamber would entertain the possibility of having session -- being in session tomorrow afternoon or whether that's a possibility or not. We have gotten a bit behind this week, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that we could not find a courtroom tomorrow afternoon. So we could only sit in the morning session, which is that -- till 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President. I thought I had to ask. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
